rv.q: Mr. Cumming's solo 'Macbeth' is a tour de force of acting that transforms Shakespeare's shortest tragedy into an unexpectedly intimate theatrical experience.
Cumming delivering a tour-de-force performance that holds the audience captive for 70 intermissionless minutes.
In a sad, emotionally draining and bravura perf, he makes it seem as if every psychosis and hallucination in the play is an expression of one man’s fragile state of mind.

While there is no doubt about Cumming's ability - he cowers, he acts menacing, he strips down, he leaps in and out of a full bathtub and smears himself in gore - there is a feeling that while this is an act of Olympic skill, it's also partly a freak show

His is a tragic hero without drive; a protagonist who forgets whose name is on the marquee; a reactive, overly inactive Macbeth, looking to slide into a role that, for all the play's famous nihilism, still must be one of driving all the trouble out there on the heath.

But while the stylishly eerie trappings (the grungy sterility of the set, by Merle Hensel, is enough to give you the willies) and Mr. Cumming’s energetic flitting among characters keep us constantly entertained, the staging accrues little in the way of dramatic intensity or emotional power.
While this Macbeth has spooky atmosphere and the verse raises gooseflesh, it falls between camps.
But what a tour-de-force performance it is.
Despite Cumming’s extreme commitment, intricate lighting effects and an eerie soundscape, this “Macbeth” is essentially just a glorified acting exercise.
In addition to his martial and co-directing skills, Branagh delivers one of the most incisive and detailed portrayals of the role in recent memory.

Other than providing a tour-de-force challenge for an actor, however, the point of this production escapes me.
